reasoning: Both outputs are strong Dev-Team PRDs that skip discovery, reject open rate as a metric, mandate a holdout, and group open questions by owner. A wins on engineering-readiness and technical precision. A's decisive edge is its Section 0 Assumptions & Decisions Log: eight decisions (D1-D8) each with rationale AND cost-to-reverse, which resolves the tension between 'don't silently invent' and 'engineering needs it Monday' better than B's approach of leaving items open. A neither invents silently (every call is logged and overturnable in one line) nor leaves the build blocked. B, by contrast, defers several P0-shaped questions that engineering needs on day one: item/project caps (R-A4 [NEEDS INPUT]), ramp schedule (R-C7 [NEEDS INPUT]), default on/off (R-E3 [NEEDS INPUT]), dormancy threshold (R-B4), and most consequentially the timezone/batch architecture (OQ-3, which B itself calls 'highest-cost' and says 'blocks the batch architecture'). A decides all of these and marks them reversible. A also carries substantially more buildable specification: an explicit event taxonomy table with in-v1 flags and per-event collapse rules (B has no equivalent at all — R-A1 just says 'source from the activity stream'), a half-open window interval [start, cutoff) to prevent boundary double-count/drop, a timezone-offset snapshot at scheduling time, an idempotency key (user_id, digest_period_id), a concrete rollout ramp (internal/1/10/50/100 with spam-rate gates at each), a permission regression test as a named release gate, and 16 edge cases vs B's 10. On accuracy, A's regulatory detail is tighter: it states the Gmail 0.3% consequence precisely (loss of mitigation eligibility until under for 7 consecutive days) and cites CASL's 10-business-day bar, whereas B overstates enforcement ('Google, Yahoo, Microsoft and Apple now enforce... with hard rejection rather than spam-foldering' conflates auth failure with spam-rate breach, and overstates Apple's role as a bulk-sender enforcer). B has two genuine advantages worth naming: (1) requirement IDs (R-A1, R-B3, R-C2...) that make the doc directly ticketable and let open questions cite the exact requirement they block, which is a real Dev-Team usability win A lacks; and (2) the RFC 8058 DKIM-signing-order gotcha (headers added after signing are not covered, so providers ignore them) — a sharp implementation catch A misses. B is also marginally cleaner on not re-litigating: A opens with three lines of 'weekly digest email is a solution, not a problem' pushback, though it immediately accepts the call and proceeds, so the expectation still passes. B's stress test lands one point A misses (variable send volume from empty-digest suppression means the primary metric needs exposure-adjustment, not a naive arm comparison). Net: B is better organized for ticketing; A is better specified, more accurate, and more decision-ready for a Monday handoff. Completeness and correctness outweigh traceability here, so A takes it — clearly, though not overwhelmingly.

strengths: Section 0 Assumptions & Decisions Log with per-decision rationale and cost-to-reverse — lets the reader overturn any call in one line while leaving nothing blocked
Explicit event taxonomy table (in-v1 flag + collapse rule per event type); B has no equivalent
Two governing rules stated as rules: render net state not the event stream, and authorize at render time against current ACLs
Precise window semantics: half-open interval plus timezone offset snapshotted at scheduling time, so boundary weeks neither double-count nor drop
Idempotency key (user_id, digest_period_id) plus failure isolation, retry abandonment after cutoff+24h, and a kill switch tested in staging before first send
Concrete rollout ramp with a spam-rate gate at every step, rather than deferring the ramp
Permission regression test named as a release gate, with the exact fixture case (user removed mid-window yields zero rows)

Metrics table is the more measurable of the two: every metric has an instrumentable definition, guardrails carry proposed numeric thresholds with stop conditions, and open rate is called out as explicitly NOT a metric with the MPP reason
14 open questions grouped by owner (Product/Legal/Engineering/Design/Data), each naming what it changes
Regulatory detail is accurate and specific: CAN-SPAM primary-purpose test turned into a hard template constraint, CASL 10-business-day bar, Gmail 0.1%/0.3% with the correct consequence
16 edge cases including several B misses (item created and deleted in-window, org disables between generation and send, untranslated locale, missed window entirely)
Stress test names the highest-leverage reframe ('what needs her' vs 'what changed'), critiques its own holdout design, and ends with the cheapest next action
weaknesses: Requirements are bullets under lettered subsections with no per-requirement IDs, so engineering cannot cite 'R-B3' in a ticket the way B allows
Opens with three lines of pushback on the problem framing before the doc; it accepts the decision immediately, but it is still a small detour the prompt asked to skip
Longest document of the two (~364 lines); density is earned but the Monday reader has more to get through
Misses the RFC 8058 DKIM-signing-order implementation bug that B catches
Does not address that suppressing empty digests makes exposure counts unequal across arms, which complicates the primary-metric comparison (B catches this)

strengths: Per-requirement IDs (R-A1 ... R-F4) make the doc directly ticketable and let dependencies, risks, and open questions cite exact requirements — the strongest structural feature in either document
Open questions are ordered by what they block, each stating whether it gates the build or only the first send, so Monday's work can start against the unblocked majority
Catches the RFC 8058 DKIM-signing-order bug: List-Unsubscribe headers added after signing are not covered by the signature and are ignored by providers
Send-time authorization (R-B1) correctly promoted out of edge cases and named as a security defect class, not a bug
Sharp statistical decision rule: pre-register a minimum detectable lift, p<0.05 sustained over 6 consecutive sends, with the reasoning for 6
Suppression rate used as a diagnostic — near 0% means the relevance filter is too loose — which is a genuinely good inverted metric
Counter-metric (all-email opt-out, not just digest opt-out) clearly explains why it is the metric that catches the real damage
R-A4 justifies the cap requirement with Gmail's ~102KB clipping threshold, so the cap is argued even where the number is open
Explicitly declines to draw a legal conclusion and routes it to OQ-1 while building to the stricter standard regardless — a clean separation of platform fact from legal judgment
Cleanest handling of the prompt's framing: names the audience cue and the closed build decision in the first two sentences and parks the residual risk in the stress test
weaknesses: Leaves five build-relevant parameters as [NEEDS INPUT] that A decides-and-flags: item/project caps, ramp schedule, default on/off, dormancy threshold, and subject-line copy

OQ-3 (local timezone vs single global batch) is left open despite B's own admission it 'blocks the batch architecture' — the single largest architectural unknown handed to engineering unresolved for a Monday start

No event taxonomy: R-A1 points at 'the persisted project activity stream' without specifying which event types are in v1 or how each collapses, leaving the highest-volume design question to implementation
No window-boundary semantics (open vs half-open interval), so consecutive weeks can double-count or drop events at the cutoff

Overstates bulk-sender enforcement: 'Google, Yahoo, Microsoft and Apple now enforce bulk-sender rules with hard rejection rather than spam-foldering' conflates authentication failure with spam-rate breach, and Apple is not a bulk-sender enforcer in that sense
Two guardrail thresholds (unsubscribe rate, hard bounce rate) and the holdout percentage are unset, weakening the measurability of the guardrail set
Thinner edge-case coverage (10 vs 16); misses create-and-delete-in-window, org-level disable between generation and send, untranslated locale, and missed send window
Stress test is shorter and does not surface an alternative framing of the product itself
